support_summary: D6/D8: all references were independently evaluated by 2 investigators with discrepancies resolved by consensus but, as the authors note, no inter-rater reliability statistic was calculated, and counts are pooled across the 3 prompt types with per-prompt-group results printed only as mean accuracy scores (Table 1 vs Table 3); fabricated was defined as not found in PubMed, Google Scholar or CrossRef, with 0/1/2 accuracy counts printed per model (Tables 3-4). || A2: Overall some concerns: verification across PubMed/Google Scholar/CrossRef with DOI errors reported apart (D4/D7 low) and duplicate independent evaluation resolved by consensus (D6 some concerns - an inter-rater statistic was explicitly not calculated), but the 10 queries are author-chosen with no sampling frame (D1), prompt wordings are summarised rather than verbatim (D2), and prompt-group results appear only as mean scores without counts (D8).

D2: Bard, Perplexity, SciSpace, Elicit and Bing are named with no version strings and no generation date is stated, so the run cannot be placed in time (Methods); verifier identity and duplicate verification are never reported, and no whole-reference fabricated count is printed - only RHS identifier errors against PubMed/Google Scholar (Tables 2-3). || A2: Overall high on D2: the six chatbots are named by family only (ChatGPT 3.5, Perplexity, SciSpace, Elicit, Bing, Bard) with no versions, no generation date and no interface stated, so the run cannot be repeated or placed in time; D5/D6 are also no information and no whole-reference fabricated counts are printed (D7/D8).

D1/D2/D3: topics were 50 ChatGPT-suggested proposals screened by five reviewers against FINER criteria, model is named only as ChatGPT (GPT-3) with no generation date, and no generation settings are reported; verification was strong - five researchers independently checked Scopus/PubMed/Google search, discrepancies discussed and resolved, Fleiss kappa 0.959 (Results; Table 3). || A2: Overall high on D1/D2: the 50 topics were suggested by ChatGPT itself and then FINER-filtered for novelty (a thin-literature lean, with re-prompting contemplated if topics failed), and the drafting run is reported only as GPT-3-era ChatGPT with no generation date; verification itself was strong (D4/D6 low: Scopus/PubMed/Google checked independently by five researchers, Fleiss kappa 0.959).

D4: fabrication was defined to include 'studies not indexed in PubMed', so verification on PubMed alone builds a coverage gap into the fabricated count itself (Results; Appendix C Table 4); each of the 5 graders also evaluated only citations from responses they themselves generated (single grader per response, element-by-element PubMed match, any discrepancy including minor typographical errors counted equally), though topics were all 70 AAOS CPG recommendations, prompts are in Appendix A, and runs were February-March 2026 on paid ChatGPT-5 with web search available under default settings. || A2: Overall high on D4: PubMed is the sole verification source and hallucination is defined to include real studies 'not indexed in PubMed', so patterned misses are counted as fabrication by rule; each grader also verified only the citations generated in their own responses (D5) with no duplicate check possible (D6), despite the complete AAOS guideline frame (D1 low) and per-CPG counts in Appendix C (D8 low).

D1: two prompt versions were tested for each request and 'the query that led to the largest number of results was retained', i.e. the prompt was selected after seeing outputs (Methods); verifier identity and duplicate verification for the LLM-supplied papers are not reported (the two independent reviewers screened the PubMed systematic-review search only), and 'hallucinated' was defined as any 2 of title, first author or year wrong (Abstract; Table 2). || A2: Overall high on D3: of the two prompt versions run for each request, 'the query that led to the largest number of results was retained', so the analysed outputs were selected after seeing the results; D5/D6 are also no information for verification of the LLM outputs (the two independent reviewers screened the systematic reviews, not the generated papers).

D4/D7: verification was against PubMed alone, so references outside PubMed could be missed, and 'Non-Correct Citations' fold unrelated real references in with unfindable ones without a split (Summary; Table 1); duplicate verification itself was sound - two ophthalmology experts independently validated citations in phase 2 with Cohen kappa 0.74. || A2: Overall some concerns with no domain high: D4 rests on PubMed as the single named verification database (partly mitigated by the expert second phase), D1 uses author-selected anterior-segment texts from one textbook, and D2/D3/D6 carry reporting gaps; D5/D7/D8 are low (two independent ophthalmology experts, Cohen kappa 0.74; predefined error categories with counts apart).

D6: citation validity 'was assessed by a single evaluator' with specialty training and the authors state no inter-rater reliability testing was conducted (Results, citation hallucination assessment; Limitations); verification sources were strong (PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science, publisher databases, doi.org) across the full 331-question AAP examination set, but the Results text mislabels the GPT-5.0 IQ arm as 'GPT-4.0 IQ' (Table 5). || A2: Overall high on D6: citation validity was assessed by a single evaluator with no inter-rater reliability testing (stated in the paper), using a judgement-based three-tier taxonomy, so one verifier's calls set the rates alone; the 331-question AAP examination frame (D1) and multi-source verification including doi.org and publisher databases (D4) are low.

D5/D6/D3: paper never states who verified the 59 references, whether verification was duplicated or blinded, or any generation settings (Methods; Results); topics were 20 author-chosen medical questions, and only 11 of 18 real references were journal articles, leaving handling of the other real references unclear, though existence was checked on PubMed and journal websites. || A2: Overall high by the combination rule: D3/D6 no information (generation settings and any duplicate or blinded verification are undescribed) plus five domains at some concerns leaves verification unchecked; D7 is low (fabricated 41/59 with minor-error n=3 and major-error n=5 counts apart in the table).

D1: 120 questions author-developed across 8 radiology subspecialties with no external sampling frame (Methods; Supplementary Material 1); all other domains low - verbatim prompt presented December 2024 with default parameters, Radiologist 1 blinded and did not pose the questions, RAS 0=fabricated defined against Medline/Google Scholar/DOAJ/web searches (Table 2). || A2: All domains low: 120 questions across 8 subspecialties listed in supplement, full prompt printed (Fig 2), exact model versions with December 2024 default-parameter runs and first complete response only, and blinded evaluation by Radiologist 1, who did not pose the questions, against Medline/Google Scholar/DOAJ/web searches with RAS category counts in Table 2.

D2: DeepSeek is named with no version and no generation date is stated for either model (Table 3; section 3.5); a single conjunctivitis topic was used, verifier identity and duplication are unreported, and further errors (incomplete author lists, wrong issue/volume numbers) are described in text without counts, so partial matches are not counted apart. || A2: Overall high on D2/D7: DeepSeek is unversioned and ChatGPT is given only as 4.0, with no generation date and no citation-task prompt reported, and no near-match rule is stated (the hallucination rate is defined as fake-or-inaccurate over total while Table 3 counts 'Fake references'); D1/D3/D5/D6 are also no information.

D1/D7/D4: three ad-hoc topics were probed in interactive conversations in which the model was confronted and re-prompted after its answers were seen, including a request for literature by co-author A. Kleyer (Main text; Figure 1); no verification source is named ('independent literature search' only - PubMed/Scopus/Web of Science appear only inside the quoted AI reply), model version is not stated, and no rule for partially matching references is given, with verifiers being the two authors who ran the chats. || A2: Overall high on D1/D2/D7: four ad-hoc requests (rare-disease off-label letter, prodromal RA, co-author Kleyer's own literature, JAK-inhibition risks) with iterative follow-up and confrontation prompting, no model version stated for the April 2023 experiments, no named verification source (only an 'independent literature search'; PubMed/Scopus/Web of Science appear only inside the quoted AI reply) and no partial-match rule.

D5/D6: paper never states who verified references or whether verification was duplicated or blinded - the reported Fleiss kappa measures consistency across the 3 chatbot sessions, not verifier agreement (Methods; Results Table 2); topics came from papers with at least 100 citations (established lean), prompt text is printed verbatim, sessions ran 8-10 July 2024 with a new conversation per question, and verification used PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar with six accuracy categories counted apart. || A2: Overall high by the combination rule, as for the later journal report of this design: D5/D6 no information (verifiers and any duplicate or blinded verification are undescribed; Fleiss kappa is cross-session consistency) together with D2/D3 some concerns, despite the Web of Science guideline topic frame (D1 low), three-database verification (D4 low) and full per-session category counts (D7/D8 low).

D1/D4: the 15 topic categories were themselves model-generated rather than drawn from an external frame, and bibliographic score 0 folds non-PubMed-indexed real sources (books/guidelines) in with nonexistent references, although any accessible academic database could also be checked (Methods, Reference assessment; Scoring system); verification was otherwise strong - two independent reviewers, Cohen kappa 0.966, consensus, single session March 2026 with web search enabled. || A2: Overall some concerns: reporting and checking are otherwise strong (D2/D3 low: ChatGPT-5.3 Plus in March 2026, single session, web search enabled, complete prompt-response sequence in Appendices A-C; D6 low: two independent reviewers, Cohen kappa 0.966/0.951), but the 15 topic categories were generated by the model under test itself (D1) and the score-0 category folds non-article and inaccessible sources into 'unverifiable' against a PubMed-primary source (D4).

D5/D6/D3: paper never states who verified the 176 citations or whether verification was duplicated or blinded, and no generation settings are reported (Methods; Table 1); verification source itself was strong and sequential (Google Scholar, then author-list and title searches, plus Scopus/PubMed/WorldCat), but DOI denominator differs between Table 1 (51/135) and Results text (51/141). || A2: Overall high by the combination rule: D5/D6 no information (who verified the citations and whether any duplicate or blinded check occurred is never described) together with D2/D3/D8 some concerns leaves verification unchecked, despite a strong staged multi-database search (D4 low) and a balanced familiarity-by-specificity topic design (D1 low).

D1/D8: prompts ran for 19 professors from the university hospital homepage but only the 8 professors ChatGPT recognised contributed the 260 references, and results are printed as percentages only with no counts (Main text; Table 1); prompt is printed verbatim with run dates 16-25 October 2023 and checking was by two observers against PubMed/Web of Science/Google Scholar/Lattes with consensus categorisation. || A2: Overall some concerns: the verbatim prompt, ChatGPT-4 and 16-25 October 2023 run dates are reported and verification used PubMed/Web of Science/Google Scholar/Lattes with two observers (D4 low), but results are percentages only with no counts (D7/D8) and topic-sampling, version/interface, output-handling and verifier-separation gaps remain (D1/D2/D3/D5/D6).

D5/D6/D1: two researchers both prompted ChatGPT and independently validated citations with disagreements resolved by consensus but no agreement figure reported (Methods); topics author-chosen with list in Multimedia Appendix 1; verification across Google Scholar, PubMed, Google Search and DOI Foundation (Table 2). || A2: D3 no information (no generation settings reported at all) and D1/D2/D5-D8 some concerns, but verification was itself checked (D4 low: Google Scholar+PubMed+Google Search plus DOI Foundation validation; D6 duplicate independent validation resolved by consensus), so overall some concerns; topics were author-selected with niche/sensitive topics excluded and only a sample prompt is given in Multimedia Appendix 1.

D4/D5/D6: no verification source is named anywhere and verifier identity, independence and duplication are all unreported, so fabrication calls (complete vs partial, Methods; Tables 4-5) cannot be checked against a stated source; topics were the full 192-question OrthoBullets SAE set, and video items were excluded because of Copilot limitations. || A2: Overall high: verification is entirely undocumented (D4/D5/D6 no information - no verification source, verifier or duplicate check is named anywhere in the paper), so the real/partially/completely fabricated counts cannot be checked, although the category definitions and per-model counts are fully reported (D7/D8 low).

D5/D6: paper never states who verified references or whether verification was duplicated or blinded - the reported Fleiss kappa measures consistency of chatbot answers across the 3 sessions, not verifier agreement (Table 4; Table 2 testing schedule); topics derived from papers with at least 100 citations lean to established guideline areas, while prompt text and per-arm testing dates are printed. || A2: Overall high by the combination rule: D5/D6 no information (who verified the 1,947 references and whether any duplicate or blinded check occurred is never stated; the reported Fleiss kappa measures cross-session consistency, not verifier agreement) together with D2/D3 some concerns; the topic frame (D1), three-database verification (D4), six-category counts (D7) and complete arm reporting (D8) are low.

D2: model is named only as 'ChatGPT (free version)' with no version string and no generation date, and generation settings are never reported (temperature is raised only as a limitation); questions came from the Japanese Physical Therapy Guidelines (5 per section x 3 sections), references were checked by PMID/DOI then title searches on an unnamed database, with two assessors per section and weighted kappa 0.93-0.98 for reference accuracy, though section denominators sum to 38 against a text total of 37 (Table 2). || A2: Overall some concerns: questions were randomly extracted from the Japanese Physical Therapy Guidelines and the verbatim prompt and 3 April 2023 data-collection date are given (D1 low), and references were checked via PMID/DOI then title search by two assessors per section with weighted kappa 0.93-0.98 for references (D4/D6 low), but the free-version model is not pinned to an exact version (D2) and section denominators sum to 38 against a text total of 37 (D7/D8).

D1: the 10 neurocritical care topics were 'selected by a single domain expert without a formal consensus or Delphi process' and not stratified by evidence density (authors' Limitations); every other domain is low - identical zero-shot prompts on 10 March 2026 via official paid interfaces with retrieval disabled, and two blinded neurocritical care experts independently verified each reference against PubMed, DOI resolver, Google Scholar and CrossRef with Cohen kappa 0.91 and a stated 0-3 Hallucination Scale (Methods; Table 1). || A2: Overall some concerns, driven only by D1/D2: the 10 neurocritical care topics were selected by a single domain expert without stratification (the paper's own stated limitation) and the verbatim prompt wording is described and diagrammed (Fig 1) rather than reproduced in text, while settings, verification and checking are exemplary (D3-D8 low: retrieval disabled, no regeneration, four sources including DOI resolver, two blinded experts, Cohen kappa 0.91).

D5/D6/D8: verification was programmatic against Crossref and PubMed APIs with printed verified/warning/failed/corrupted categories (Table 3), but there was no independent human duplicate check, three arms used unreported system-default models, the authors' own AI Research Army system is one of the arms under test, and several printed hallucination rates do not equal (failed+corrupted)/total from the printed counts (section 3.4). || A2: Overall some concerns: verification is programmatic and rule-based (D4 low: Crossref and PubMed APIs, exact title matching with Levenshtein <=3 fallback, logged timestamps; D7 verified/warning/failed/corrupted counts apart), but the authors benchmark their own AI Research Army system (D5), three comparator systems run on unreported system-default models (D2), and several printed hallucination rates do not match the printed counts (D8).

D6/D1: reference validation was by a single reviewer with, as the authors state, no inter-rater reliability data, using judgement-based classes (fabricated, misrepresented, accurate/supportive) whose fabricated and misrepresented counts are not printed separately - only the combined 29/88 hallucination count (Table 1; Results, Reference reliability); validation covered a correctness-stratified subsample (all 44 incorrect answers plus 44 randomly selected correct answers) of the 203 OITE questions, with GPT-5 run 29-30 August 2025 at default temperature 1.0 in a new chat per question and checked on PubMed, Google Scholar, Google and librarian-assisted searches. || A2: Overall some concerns: generation and verification sources are strong (D1-D4 low: all 203 OITE questions, verbatim prompt, GPT-5 accessed 29-30 August 2025 via web interface with temperature left at default 1.0, PubMed/Google Scholar/Google plus hospital library), but validation rests on a single reviewer with no inter-rater data (D5/D6) and fabricated versus misrepresented counts are never split, with the 33% hallucination rate pooled from a stratified subsample of 88 responses (D7/D8).

D2/D5/D6: no model versions are stated for ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity (data collected 1-30 September 2025 on free-tier web interfaces, Methods) and all RHS scoring was by a single investigator, mitigated by a predefined rubric, a standardised PubMed/Google Scholar workflow and 95% intra-rater agreement on a random 200-reference re-check (Supplementary Material); no fabricated or accurate counts are printed, only RHS means (Tables 2-4). || A2: Overall some concerns with no domain high: outcomes are RHS means only with no fabricated or accurate counts for any arm (D7/D8), models are unversioned family names (D2; September 2025 dates and free-tier web interfaces are stated), and scoring was by a single investigator with only an intra-rater recheck of a random 200 references at 95% agreement (D5/D6); all three chatbots and both formats are reported.

D5/D7: references were cross-checked independently by two reviewers on PubMed, Google Scholar and Web of Science with discrepancies resolved by discussion but no agreement statistic, and author contributions show one verifier (DS) also generated the prompts and collected the data (Methods, Reference verification; Table 6); 'False' (n=61) folds fabricated and unverifiable references together with irrelevant real ones, with no split printed. || A2: Overall some concerns: guideline-based MIH questions, three-database cross-checks and blinded duplicate verification resolved to full agreement are strengths (D1/D4/D6/D8 low), but the generation date and settings are unreported (D2/D3), one verifier also generated the prompts and collected the data per the contributions statement (D5), and the binary True/False code folds irrelevant real references into the 'fake' counts (D7).

D7/D8: references were classified as verifiable, inaccurate or hallucinated under a stated rule (Methods 3.3) but per-model hallucinated counts are not printed - only per-question hallucination-rate ranges - and inaccurate counts are not given apart per model (Results 4.1); sampling was systematic (first 200 Quora rosacea questions screened by predefined criteria), models are exactly versioned with web search disabled and default configuration, and the evaluating dermatologist was blinded to model identity. || A2: Overall high on D6/D8: each evaluation domain, including reference verification, was performed by a single designated expert with no inter-rater check, and per-model hallucinated counts are not printed at all (only per-question ranges: Claude hallucination in 1 of 6 citing questions; ChatGPT-5.2 18.2-50.0%; DeepSeek-V3.2 10.0-58.3%), although sampling, exact versions, dates and settings are fully reported (D1-D5 low).
